explanation: Double-quoted strings support variable interpolation and escape sequences (e.g., \n, \t), while single-quoted strings treat content literally except for escaped single quotes and backslashes — it's not just a speed difference.
The ?? operator is syntactic sugar for isset() and returns the fallback value without raising warnings or notices for undefined variables.
In PHP, echo accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and concatenates them without any separator.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always evaluates to 1 and can be used in expressions, e.g. $x = print 'hello'; assigns 1 to $x.
The elvis operator (?:) returns the left operand when it is truthy, not when it is falsy.
In PHP, the concatenation operator (.) has lower precedence than arithmetic operators like + and -, so '1' + 2 . '3' is parsed as (1+2) . '3'.
The ** operator in PHP is right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not 64.
The + operator has higher precedence than ., so it's parsed as 'sum: ' . (2+3), which concatenates 'sum: ' with 5 to give 'sum: 5'.
With ===, arrays are equal only if they have the same key/value pairs in the same order; order matters with strict comparison.
In PHP, false is cast to 0 when compared with an integer using ==, so 0 == 0 evaluates to true.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to an integer converts the integer to a string for comparison, so 'abc' == 0 becomes 'abc' == '0', which is false.
In PHP loose comparison (==), null is equal to 0, '', and false — all three comparisons return true.
PHP's (int) cast parses leading numeric characters and stops at the first non-numeric character, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP coerces the numeric string '5' to the integer 5, then performs 5 + 5 = 10.
In PHP, casting false to a string results in an empty string "", not "0".
0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004 due to floating-point precision, so strict equality with 0.3 is false.
strrev() reverses byte-by-byte, which breaks multi-byte UTF-8 characters; use strrev with mbstring or a proper UTF-8-aware reversal instead.
str_checks('Hello world', 'world') returns true because 'world' is a substring of 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right, left, or both sides, controlled by the pad_type parameter (STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
The default character mask for trim() is " \t\n\r\0\x0B", which includes spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen counts bytes; 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so h(1)+é(2)+l(1)+l(1)+o(1)=6.
substr('abcdef', -3) starts at the 3rd character from the end, returning the last 3 characters 'def'.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; it does not modify the original string in place.
Heredoc supports variable interpolation, while nowdoc (with single-quoted delimiter) treats content as a plain string with no interpolation.
The sort() function does NOT preserve key associations; it reindexes the array. The asort() function is the one that preserves key-to-value associations.
In PHP, string keys that are valid integer representations (e.g., '5') are automatically cast to integers when used as array keys.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; the third parameter $strict must be set to true to use strict comparison (===).
Without a callback, array_filter() removes elements that evaluate to false (0, '0', '', null, false, []).
The third parameter $preserve_keys defaults to false, meaning array_slice() re-indexes keys starting from 0 by default.
array_slice starting at offset 1 with length 2 returns elements at index 1 and 2, which are 20 and 30.
Array union (+) keeps left-side values for duplicate keys and appends new keys from the right, resulting in ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2].
Since PHP 8.1, the array spread operator officially supports arrays with string keys, which previously would trigger a warning.
PHP does allow combining named arguments with argument unpacking in a single call, e.g. foo(a: 1, ...$named, c: 3).
In PHP, closures do not automatically inherit variables from the outer scope; you must explicitly import them using the 'use' keyword.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments passed to the function call, which is 3, regardless of how many parameters are declared in the signature.
An arrow function's body is always a single expression after the => operator, not multiple expressions in curly braces.
PHP arrow functions (fn) automatically capture outer variables by value, unlike closures which capture by reference by default.
In PHP, a static closure does not capture $this from the surrounding scope, unlike a regular closure which does.
The 'use ($x)' clause captures the value of $x (5) by value at closure creation time, so later reassignment to 7 does not affect it.
In coercive (weak) typing mode, PHP will attempt to convert the string '5' to the integer 5 when it is passed to an int-typed parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility and type declarations directly in constructor parameters to automatically create class properties.
In PHP, the 'final' keyword before a method declaration prevents subclasses from overriding that method.
In PHP, the 'final' keyword prevents a method from being overridden in any subclass.
Private properties in PHP are only accessible within the class that defines them, not in subclasses.
Private methods are not visible to child classes, so they are not part of the inheritance contract; a child can declare a method with the same name and any visibility without conflict.
__get() is called for any inaccessible property, including both non-existent and existing but private/protected properties accessed from outside the class.
Reassigning a readonly property in PHP throws a ReadOnlyProperty error, which is a subclass of \Error.
PHP interfaces can declare constants, which are always public and immutable.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or interface.
Starting from PHP 8.0, interfaces are allowed to declare static methods.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so it does not ignore interfaces.
In PHP, interface methods are implicitly abstract and cannot have a body (default implementation); that is a feature of traits and abstract classes.
In PHP, abstract methods can be declared as public or protected, but not private, since they must be accessible for implementation in child classes.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all three defined cases: A, B, and C.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError inherits from Error, not Exception; they are siblings under the Throwable interface.
The @ operator suppresses errors (E_WARNING, E_NOTICE, etc.) but does not suppress exceptions; exceptions must be caught with try/catch.
intdiv(5, 0) throws a DivisionByZeroError exception in PHP 7+.
In PHP, the finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception is caught or not; it runs before the exception propagates upward.
An exception thrown in a finally block replaces any exception being propagated from the try or catch block, so it does have an effect on the result.
Shutdown functions registered via register_shutdown_function() are called whenever the script terminates, including when exit or die is called.

The use statement is a compile-time alias that simply maps a short name to a fully qualified class name; the actual file is only loaded when the class is first used at runtime (triggering the autoloader).
In PHP, to import a function via a use statement, you prefix it with the keyword 'function', e.g., use function Foo\Bar\myFunc;
PSR-4 strips the 'App\' prefix, converts remaining namespace separators to directories, and appends .php to the base path src/.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php calls spl_autoload_register() to register its ClassLoader with PHP's SPL autoloader stack.
__NAMESPACE__ is a PHP magic constant (since PHP 5.3) that returns the current namespace as a string, or an empty string if no namespace is defined.
An unqualified class name in 'new' is resolved relative to the current namespace, not from the global root; only a leading backslash forces global root resolution.
PSR-4 maps the base namespace 'App\' to 'src/', and the remaining sub-namespace 'Model\User' directly translates to the file path src/Model/User.php.
PHP allows use statements inside function bodies, and the alias then only applies within that function's scope.
In PHP, arrays are value types and are copied on assignment, unlike objects which are passed by reference (handle).
PHP arrays are copied by value on assignment, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which remains [1, 2].
In PHP, variables defined in the global scope are not directly accessible inside a function unless explicitly imported via the global keyword, accessed through $GLOBALS, or passed as parameters.
unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the variable from the global scope entirely, not just for the current function.
The parameter is passed by reference, so $n is incremented from 5 to 6.
A foreach by value iterates over an internal copy of the array, so changes made to the array inside the loop body are not reflected in the current iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances, not tied to any single object.
In PHP, boolean array keys are cast to integers (true becomes 1, false becomes 0), so they are stored as int, not bool.
Since PHP 7.1, generators support return with a value, retrievable via $gen->getReturn() after the generator is exhausted.
Once a generator is fully consumed it is closed, and calling rewind() on it throws a RuntimeException: 'Cannot rewind a closed generator.'
yield from is a Python construct; PHP only has yield, not yield from.
Calling a generator function (one containing yield) returns a Generator object, so get_class() on it returns the string 'Generator'.
The generator yields 1, 2, 3 via yield from, iterator_to_array converts it to a 3-element array, and count returns 3.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last In, First Out) stack; SplQueue is the one that implements FIFO.
ArrayIterator is a built-in PHP class that wraps an array and implements the Iterator interface, allowing traversal via methods like current(), next(), key(), valid(), and rewind().
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a random salt and embeds it in the returned hash string; there is no parameter to supply a custom salt.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is PASSWORD_BCRYPT, not MD5.
password_verify compares the plain text 'secret' against the hash of 'secret', which naturally matches, so it returns true.
strip_tags() removes HTML/XML tags from a string and helps mitigate XSS, but SQL injection is prevented by using prepared statements or proper escaping, not by stripping tags.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID to invalidate the old one, which is the standard defense against session fixation attacks, typically called upon login.
php_sapi_name() returns the name of the loaded SAPI module, such as 'cli', 'apache2', or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() only removes the session data on the server; to remove the PHPSESSID cookie from the browser, you must explicitly call setcookie() with a past expiration time.
The $_SESSION array is only populated with session data after calling session_start(); without it, $_SESSION is an empty or undefined array.
PHP names anonymous classes with 'class@anonymous' followed by file and line info; the short/class name portion is 'class@anonymous'.
In PHP, traits can declare constants, which are accessible in any class that uses the trait.
In PHP, casting any object (including an Exception instance) to bool always yields true.
The array_find() function was introduced in PHP 8.3.
Property hooks (get/set in property declarations) were introduced in PHP 8.4.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g. `public private(set) string $name`) was indeed introduced in PHP 8.4.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing developers to mark function results that must not be silently ignored.
The pipe operator (|>) was introduced as an experimental feature in PHP 8.4.
The 'Clone with' feature, allowing object cloning with property overrides, was accepted for PHP 8.4.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were introduced in PHP 8.4 as part of the new array helper functions.
The RFC Partial Function Application v2 was adopted for PHP 8.5.
The clamp() function was introduced in PHP 8.4 via the RFC clamp_v2.
The RFC Context Managers v2 was adopted into PHP, providing a mechanism for scoped context management.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC was accepted, not declined; it was a revised proposal following the rejection of the earlier Generic Types RFC.
PHP has not adopted an RFC to enable ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) by default; the standard build remains NTS (Non-Thread Safe).
PHP 8.5 still does not include native generics (parameterized types); they remain absent despite long-standing community requests and workarounds like @template annotations for static analysis.
PHP major releases occur in mid-November; PHP 8.5 would have been released in November 2025, and PHP 8.6's GA on 2026-11-19 means it is not yet out as of 2026-11-06, making 8.5 the latest stable.
PHP 6 was planned but never released; the versioning went directly from PHP 5.6 to PHP 7.0.
The RFC for adding a #[\Deprecated] attribute to PHP core was not adopted; it was rejected, unlike #[\Override] which was accepted for PHP 8.3.
